There was hope on offer too, in organizations holding nonprofit housing and government officials accountable for taking public money and paying staff while single room occupancy homes stay as they are. Without rent control and a concerted effort between government and private enterprise, a growing city pushes more people into being unhoused.
beats.pullQuote: you can't apply for employment unless you have an address, but because they're unhoused, they don't have an address
beats.slideHint: The August 2024 storyboard six-panel with the housing question at the top, and the international examples named in the applications panel: Finland rent caps, New York City across generations, Hampton Roads off-post housing. Beside it a small cycle diagram, no address to no job to no housing to no address, and an update strip for the Downtown Eastside nonprofits and the accountability organizations.

beats.title: A question left standing, then mentoring adolescents
beats.summary: The housing round produced one question: what incentive, if any, a city like Vancouver offers a private owner of a multifamily building to open a share of units to people in the situation just described. No answer came. After a long silence the response was that the topic is difficult, that the storyboard would keep being updated, and that this is not only Vancouver but any large population center where public and private sectors fail to act together. The questioner then asked whether they had been heard at all, having spoken at length unsure the mute button was off. They had been. The format absorbed the question rather than resolving it, which is what the format is for. The next storyboard was 15 September 2024, on how we mentor adolescents into adulthood. Theories: balance in parenting, guiding children with freedom that is not absolute; constant cultivation, moving a child through a checklist of life skills such as swimming, martial arts and the Scouts as the measure of preparation; and technology as a surrogate educator, supplying information that is sometimes validated and sometimes not. Applications: responsibility thrust on children early, by design or through unfortunate circumstance; living abroad in Germany increasing the opportunity for autonomy; Japan, where young children walking to and from school alone is a strict cultural norm from early elementary age; and in the United States a gap in access to caregivers created by design, where training and deployments leave a family with an absent caregiver and a condition for poverty. Sources and input: negotiation as a life skill, and the question of when children get to negotiate with caregivers for more autonomy, which arrives at different stages in different families; and access to quality mentors, including whether surrogate mentors arrive from extended family or local community when a caregiver is absent, and whether that absence seeds harmful coping mechanisms carried into adulthood. Policies: flexible work options and paid time off for employees with children as a route to parental involvement at school and in community events, rather than family time confined to weekends and holidays. Opportunities and challenges: what volunteer mentorship exists around schools and communities; which social media platforms are of higher quality, and when to start guiding children toward a safe presence online; learning what today's youth actually like so they can be met on their own terms rather than taught what their elders were taught; and a shortage of mentors in every community.
beats.pullQuote: allows us to guide children by giving freedom, but not absolute freedom.
beats.slideHint: Split slide. Left, a single unanswered question in a box: what incentives does a city give a private multifamily owner to open units, carried forward. Right, the September 2024 storyboard six-panel with the mentoring question at the top, constant cultivation and technology as surrogate educator named in theories, and Germany and Japan set against the United States caregiver gap in applications.

beats.title: What mentorship actually looks like
beats.summary: This inquiry's call to action had been taken by two participants, one of them absent. The absent one had planned to use social media and research to see how different communities address mentorship, from the local level up to the international. The other had offered to find organizations that encourage mentorship and good examples worth copying, and gave the report. A general internet search turns up a plethora of organizations, most of them aimed at at-risk youth and most concentrated on high school age. Named were the YMCA, behavioral health services in various states, the Up Center, the Boys and Girls Club of America, and Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts as a form of mentorship in themselves. The pattern is consistent: a mentor signs up, picks a mentee, and commits a couple of hours a week, under a state, federal or city programme, inside a school system, or through a nonprofit. The clearest example found was the Up Center's Team Up, running since 2008 for ages 6 to 17. Mentorship also tends to be rooted in whatever activity is already in a person's life: the volunteer became a certified official with USA Swimming and now gives monthly hours to officiating meets. One avenue named but not yet pursued was a school-based youth programme. Beyond programmes, the report was about ordinary conversation, asking young people why they do what they do, why they attend to social media, what they are studying, and what they intend after high school, whether college or a vocational programme, without taking the shape of a parent. Recent graduates named a car as the first goal and had not considered putting money aside toward a house or any longer-term aim. Reading was part of the work, including the book already recorded against the work ethic inquiry. A chat contribution was read out mid-report and correctly reassigned: a Los Angeles nonprofit that empowers its community on housing rights, which belongs to the August inquiry rather than this one. The report closed with an offer to take any question from the group into further research and return with more.
beats.pullQuote: all kinds of opportunities that can stem from just simple conversations with these youths
beats.slideHint: A landscape slide of mentorship organizations as logos or plain name tiles: YMCA, state behavioral health services, the Up Center and Team Up with its 2008 start and 6 to 17 age band, Boys and Girls Club of America, Boy Scouts, Girl Scouts, USA Swimming. A sidebar headed What it takes lists a couple of hours a week, pick a mentee, start from an activity you are already in, and simple conversations about goals.

beats.title: The gap after seventeen
beats.summary: The facilitator opened the round with a question about the edge of the age band. Legal adulthood in the United States arrives at 18, and the years from 18 to 28 are a vulnerable stretch in which a young adult is answerable in law for their own decisions. The mentorship organizations named ran to 17. So do organizations continue past that line, and do any of them pass the torch across it, into the years where decisions carry legal consequences under each country's definitions. One participant, on a difficult connection, said they would have to research what exists for that age band, and confirmed the inquiry's own range as fifteen and up into adulthood. Another pushed in the opposite direction: a terrible decision at 16 can be permanent in some jurisdictions, so the plug was for earlier interdiction. It is hard to mentor a child out of a life-altering decision after the fact, and harder still from behind bars, when mentorship beforehand might have made the difference. The response accepted the point, that earlier is proactive rather than reactive, and turned it into the round's second question: how do organizations determine who counts as at-risk youth. Is it behavior already committed, or having been caught, or some other factor that marks a group as at risk before anything has gone wrong, and what criteria decide who gets mentorship and who does not.
beats.pullQuote: I hate to mentor a child after he or she has already made a life altering decision.
beats.slideHint: A timeline bar from age 6 to 28 with the mentorship programmes shaded 6 to 17, legal adulthood marked at 18, and the 18 to 28 stretch left blank and labelled as the gap. Two collected questions run underneath: who passes the torch across 18, and what criteria define at-risk before anything has happened.

beats.title: Before they leave high school
beats.summary: One participant, through a poor connection and audibly working to get the thought out, made the case for mentoring before a young person leaves high school, with a counsellor or professional based inside the school. In certain communities that person is hard to come by or not provided at all. The point was not careers advice but availability: someone there to talk to, and someone who can help a young person search for the feeling within that indicates what they might want to do. The facilitator agreed and complicated it. Student support services in Canada are one model of exactly that, but a school without those staff, or with a single guidance counsellor for an entire student body, cannot deliver it, and the result is a lack of resources to ensure students are informed or guided. Influences also depend on place: military recruiters came into the high school of a military town to pitch service after graduation, and towns without that presence have to work out for themselves which outside agencies or entities come in and hold those conversations. The note was taken for the storyboard, tied back to the earlier point that mentoring someone after a decision is already on their record is uphill work that active mentorship might have made unnecessary.
beats.pullQuote: If there's only one guidance counselor for an entire student body
beats.slideHint: A school-shaped panel listing what a young person can reach inside the building: a counsellor or support service, a teacher, an outside agency that visits. Beside it a scarcity note, one guidance counsellor for an entire student body, and a second panel contrasting a military town where recruiters visit with a town where nobody comes in at all.

beats.title: Coexistence with nature, and a note on the artifact itself
beats.summary: The last storyboard was 20 October 2024, on how we cultivate peaceful coexistence with nature in our communities. Theories and examples were international. The Ganges is a holy site to its population and is flooded with toxic waste brought by industry and by the results of religious ceremony. Venus was once like Earth until climate change altered its atmosphere and made it uninhabitable, read as a possible warning of what Earth could become without action. Applications: India using its court system to extend rights to land, water and air in the way human rights are understood; and in Virginia, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation taking a grassroots approach to building a culture of caring about a watershed regardless of a person's industry or private life. Sources and input: an uncomfortable truth, that a psychological barrier against discomfort leads people to disengage from a complex and real problem, choosing not to confront what is happening to them and limiting their own citizenship in the process; and the need for those holding the levers of power, corporations and governments, to lead by example so that communities can act. Regulations and policies: what the world looked like during and after Covid, with photographs of Los Angeles under blue sky and less smog than on a typical day before; and environmental racism, where marginalized populations face greater health hazards from unhealthy environments, unclean drinking water and land too contaminated to farm. Opportunities: increasing indigenous governance so that indigenous knowledge and wisdom shape current policy, with the David Suzuki Foundation in Canada as the example; and bringing children into nature conservation through routine play and exploration inside the regular school curriculum. Challenges: cultural wisdom requires engaging an older population about what worked for them and how to pass it on; and collectivist ideas do not resonate where thinking leans purely capitalist, which makes shaping minds toward the collective a challenge in itself. This inquiry's call to action had not moved. The planned conversation with a local beekeeper about organizing the protection of pollinators did not happen because both parties were on leave, and it was carried over, with an invitation for the beekeeper to speak briefly at a future Lyceum. The facilitator named this as the accountability part of the practice, holding each other to what was said. The co-facilitator then made an administrative point about the storyboard on screen: unlike the earlier boards, its entries are hyperlinked in blue to the sources behind them, the summaries are being hung on the website and in a few other places, copies can be sent by email on request, and the group was asked directly for ideas to improve the format. The facilitator's closing questions for the round were whether organizations inside government encourage sustainable practices and whether those examples are highlighted in a way that draws people in, and the same question of the private sector, where wealth and resources spent on sustainability may be going unreported in an atmosphere of fear that prevents shared understanding on climate change.
beats.pullQuote: People choose not to confront this as it's happening to them. So therefore, they just choose not to engage, and therefore they're limiting their citizenship in their community.
beats.slideHint: The October 2024 storyboard six-panel with the nature question at the top and its entries visibly hyperlinked in blue, the difference from earlier boards called out in a small margin note. The Ganges, Venus, India's courts, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation and the David Suzuki Foundation appear as named tiles, with the Los Angeles before and during Covid photographs paired in the policies panel. The call to action bar is marked carried forward.

beats.title: Administrative notes, and the fellowship circle
beats.summary: The website was pointed to as the place where examples of cross-cultural learning are written up so that a reader can apply them in their own community, with links there to the group's Facebook, Instagram, Twitter and Quora presence. A survey tool is in development for use in later gatherings, and until then feedback goes through the message form on the site's homepage or directly to either facilitator, on the sequence of inquiry or on this evening's sequence for reflection. Before closing, the facilitator acknowledged a reading shared in the chat on how AI may be affecting work now and in future, an essay by the chief executive of Anthropic together with a long recorded interview with the same author, confirmed that it answered the earlier question raised in the work ethic round, and assigned it to that storyboard. The fellowship circle then opened. One participant offered a visit to the Grand Canyon that week: its permanence and its age put much of what the circle discusses into proportion, and what was offered was not an answer but an open-ended thought about feeling insignificant standing beside it. Another, returning after missing the previous forum, tied the vision and purpose in the group's statement to balancing enduring truths and what is really important in life against the tyranny of a hectic present, in a period of hectic current events, and said it was good to be in the circle. Another was glad to have made this gathering after missing several, having now heard the important topics that had been missed, and hoped that as the group moves forward it will reach conclusions that help each other and the wider community. Another said they wished they could go back in time and attend the ones they had skipped. The facilitator closed by naming where the circle had joined from that night, Canada, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and Virginia, as an interconnection between different communities already in existence and a small example of what a larger version would look like, and read the motto: our lives are our own and each person walks their own path, but the journey is collective, for humanity and the natural world.
beats.pullQuote: We're all walking our path of life. But it's our collective journey.
beats.slideHint: An administrative slide with the website address, the four social media names, and a line reading survey tool in development with a feedback route. Then a closing slide holding the motto, this is your life and our journey for humanity and the natural world, over a plain map with four unlabelled markers for Canada, Los Angeles, Pittsburgh and Virginia.

beats.title: After the close: how a newcomer gets in
beats.summary: The recording continued past the formal close, with the facilitators and a newer participant staying on to work through onboarding. The problem was stated plainly. The group's video calls and collaborative work normally run on Microsoft Teams; the core few operate there at an administrative level, and new people are fitted into different levels of trust and different slots as they arrive. An onboarding team and a channel of instructions already exist, but reading them requires already being on Teams and knowing how to navigate it, which anyone outside the military or a large corporate employer that pays for the platform may not. Some in the circle are still getting used to it. What is needed is a comprehensive checklist, by the book, that can be sent to a person before they have an account, and modelled on what an incoming member actually encounters. This is the only forward-looking commitment of the evening that belongs to no inquiry.
beats.slideHint: A simple onboarding funnel: invitation by email, account created, platform basics, onboarding channel, tiers of access. Each step carries the blocker beside it, with the platform-literacy assumption marked as the point where newcomers stall, and a note that the checklist to be written must work before any account exists.

storyboard.logline: A seven-person Lyceum spanning Vancouver, Virginia and Pittsburgh took a live news item, the dissolving of the US Department of Education, and turned it into one question about what leaders owe education in their own communities.
storyboard.arcNotes: The session followed its script and still turned twice. It opened tightly - rules and norms, a pre-survey called the learning conversation, a breathing circle with gratitude to the Earth, to ancestors, to self, to family and to the next generation - and the shared understanding round showed a circle that is largely one extended family, held together by military service as much as by blood, plus two first-time guests. The first turn came when the topic arrived from the floor: not education in the abstract but the dissolving of the US Department of Education, which handed the group a live case with a Canadian comparison already in the room. The middle hour stayed unusually factual for a Lyceum, with participants supplying what they had seen rather than what they believed: every school type in one military family's life, Chile's three routes with a part-subsidized middle, a reported department budget and how little of it reaches a student, the department's real charter of equal access, its grants and non-discrimination enforcement, and the single federal intervention in standards after Sputnik. The second turn went inward, from policy to inheritance: Pittsburgh desegregated on paper in 1981 and not in fact, schools desegregated for students but not for teachers, a transfer fee that reopens sorting by income, International Baccalaureate programs sited to lift a weak school's reported scores, stipends that route teachers by need rather than fit. From there the circle asked what a government's national programs reveal about what it values, and answered that a community can decide morals, ethics and cultural identity for itself when the state will not. The last twenty minutes belonged to newcomers and to language: qualifications that stop counting at a border, language as both respect and gate, assimilation bought at the cost of a household's German. The call to action was taken up rather than assigned - how curriculum is developed, and whether parents and citizens can have a voice in it - and the fellowship circle closed on the same theme from another angle, that much of the teaching that matters is done by people who are not teachers. Contributions are recorded without names throughout: this is a record of what the circle worked through, not of who said it.

beats.title: Norms, survey, and the presence circle
beats.summary: The facilitator opened the Lyceum as an endeavor for shared purpose for families and communities, welcomed two new guests and ran an audio check with a participant who was just coming on board. The norms followed: about an hour and a half, an open forum where people come and go as life dictates, co-hosted with two others in the circle, everyone a peer whatever their walk of life, difficult and sensitive topics approached with curiosity, commonality sought while difference is acknowledged. The facilitator walked the agenda and put up the pre-survey, called the learning conversation, by chat link or QR code, describing it as a way to ground where each person is emotionally and what they may need from the group, then led the opening presence: turn sideways to open to the group and to the nature around it, lower the gaze, and five breaths, each with a prompt of gratitude.

beats.title: A world map, and the question arrives
beats.summary: The facilitator used the United Nations country map and a World Bank map that colors the world by region, suggesting the colors as a memory prompt so lived experience and cultural wisdom could be brought to bear on whatever the group chose, and explained the sequence of inquiry for the two newcomers: find a topic that matters to the group, build consensus on it, then work through theories, application in communities, what gets to the root, opportunities and challenges, and a call to action that somebody carries and reports back on, so the discussion becomes a quest rather than an evening. The floor opened. One participant proposed the role of education in communities, prompted by moves to dissolve the US Department of Education, and asked what federal and state governments each do for educating youth, and what a state-led system loses without federal support. Another answered from Canada, where the federal government has not directly funded housing for people without means since the 1990s, and added a second worry, whether the US President's talk about Canada is a joke or serious.

beats.title: Two candidate questions, and why community
beats.summary: The facilitator drafted a question on screen and drew the parallel out loud: a federal government that once provided supportive housing withdrew from it, and a department the United States has relied on may go the same way. Two avenues sat on the table, education and leadership in how messages are conveyed across countries, and the group was invited to narrow either. The facilitator explained why the group keeps saying community: the Lyceum works at the scale of towns, cities, cultural and religious groups, not capitals, because that is where decisions land on families. One participant added the group's levels of impact, from individual to family to local community, with state and federal effect a longer-term goal, and argued that what shapes daily life is settled locally: taxes, housing, food and shelter, whether a big store closes, what the gas price is. On the first candidate question the same participant admitted knowing the Department of Education only in outline, student loans, school nutrition, broad guidelines, and asked whether the leadership question could be narrowed before the group took it on.
beats.pullQuote: Now it starts to call into question, what does the government supposed to do, if anything, to empower education for communities.
beats.slideHint: Deliberation slide with the two candidate questions side by side and space to edit them live, next to a levels-of-impact diagram (individual, family, local community, state, federal) with the daily-life list beneath it: taxes, housing, food, shelter, local business, fuel prices.

beats.title: One question, chosen by consensus
beats.summary: One participant proposed folding leadership into the education question rather than dropping either, while refusing to dismiss the question of whether the President is serious about making Canada the 51st state, saying it is not always possible to tell how seriously to take what is said, that a worst-case threat analysis discounts nothing, and that weakening and disestablishing the Education Department is a long-stated aim now coming true with major effect. Analyzing that stated vision against what is actually happening in US education policy would limit the scope of both candidate questions, the same participant suggested, before wondering aloud whether the framing was too US-centric. The facilitator asked twice for objections, a raised hand or a thumbs up, took the silence as consent, and set the evening's question, noting that leaders could mean education administrators or anyone providing educational services. The theories section then opened with what people have experienced of education in a community, public, private, government or vocational.
beats.pullQuote: Looking at the question as written, what should leaders do to empower education and communities
beats.slideHint: Today's Inquiry slide - 'What should leaders do to empower education in communities?' - with a definition strip widening leaders to administrators, education services and non-formal educators, and the sequence of inquiry down the side as the evening's roadmap.

beats.title: One family, every kind of school
beats.summary: One participant offered a personal history as the first theory: public elementary, middle and high school in Norfolk, Virginia, a public university left unfinished, then a second public institution with more private elements. As a parent, the same participant has seen a private Christian school funded by tuition, parent volunteering and small overheads, run by a board to a budget; a public district school serving an installation where about ninety-nine percent of students came from the military; and Department of Defense federal schools where the funding was visible in smart boards, screens, computers, integrated technology and modern buildings. Ordinary public schools showed the reverse, a degradation of facilities and equipment, with localities choosing very different shares of city or state budget to put into a school, a quarter in one place and half in another. That participant had also taught languages in post-secondary settings in other countries, which ran differently again, and handed the question back to the group.
beats.pullQuote: So there's some major differences and some inconsistencies across the nation, at least, that I've seen
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide: a comparison table of school types (private religious, district school serving an installation, Department of Defense federal school, ordinary public school) scored on funding source, facilities, technology and oversight, with 'inconsistencies across the nation' as the banner line.

beats.title: Chile's three routes, and what the department does
beats.summary: One participant set out the Chilean system: twelve years of school then college or university, with three routes to choose from. Public schooling, a part-subsidized category where the government funds the school and the family pays half, and private, with most families reaching for the middle option because it is the affordable one. Students with strong results can attend university free, which that participant called the good part of the system, while ordinary university fees stand near the minimum wage. The open question left on the table was what actually happens in the United States if the ministry is dissolved and the responsibility passes to governors or municipalities. Another participant answered with what had been followed in the news, unverified but widely reported: overarching guidelines touching nutrition, influence with the teachers union, administration of student loans and some school funding, a back-office department with little direct influence on schools, with curriculum left to city, county or state. That participant cited a budget figure near 286 billion dollars with roughly a quarter reaching individual students, and said the rest of it remains unknown, an evolving issue nobody outside the department can call.
beats.pullQuote: the school receives money and you pay half.
beats.slideHint: Application slide 'how is this handled elsewhere': Chile's three routes as three columns (public, part-subsidized with the family paying half, private) with free university on results called out, next to a panel on what the US Department of Education actually administers and the disputed budget figure marked as unverified.

beats.title: Equal access, and who watches the states
beats.summary: One participant named the department's real charter as equal access rather than dictation to local schools, and reached back to segregation, to Alabama holding so dearly to segregated schools that the National Guard was mobilized over it, and to the phrase separate yet equal, which was simply not true. Left to their own devices, that participant argued, states may not do what is in the country's interest, and the child who never gets educated may be the one who could have cured the common cold. The same voice asked whether money saved by disestablishing the department will in fact cycle down to schools, states and local jurisdictions, and read the expression of another member of the circle as one dissenting vote. The participant whose expression had been read agreed rather than objected, and set out the programs visible through a federal department that cooperates with them: grants and priorities for underserved communities, enforced standards of equal opportunity and non-discrimination, special education criteria, developmental access, ramps and mobility devices. That participant argued that the claimed savings from shutdowns cost more than continuing the programs, that whatever remains will go to another pet project rather than back to education, and that empowering the states risks reversing fifty years of a common standard. The first speaker stepped away briefly, posting thanks in the chat.
beats.pullQuote: The child that doesn't get educated may be the one that can cure the common cold, but we don't know that because we didn't educate him or her.
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide headed 'equal access is the charter': a list of the department's programs (grants to underserved schools, non-discrimination enforcement, special education criteria, physical access), a history strip (segregation, separate yet equal, the National Guard in Alabama), and a savings-versus-shutdown-cost pair of bars.

beats.title: Transfer fees, entrance exams, no national curriculum
beats.summary: One participant agreed the money would find another department rather than return to education, dated the department's creation to 1979 with a mandate for equal attention it has not fulfilled, and gave a mechanism used first-hand: in Texas a family that can pay an added district fee and drive their child can transfer out of a Title I school to any school they like. Those who can afford it choose the better school, its ratings keep improving, and a form of segregation persists, which that participant called disproportionate to the department's intent and mostly a state-level failure. The facilitator widened the frame to China and South Korea, where entrance exams decide university places and later employment, and students study themselves almost to death for a score that can send a life either way, then named the deeper gap: Japan and Australia teach a national curriculum and the United States does not, so history and what it means to be American are interpreted school by school, which the facilitator read as a national identity crisis underneath the polarization. A third participant posted in the chat that this was the start of separate but equal.
beats.pullQuote: there's almost like there's a national identity crisis. It's like, Hey, what does it mean to be an American?
beats.slideHint: Two panels: 'shifting to the better school' with the added district fee, the ratings loop and the funding that follows the scores; and 'national curriculum' comparing Japan and Australia with the United States, with the entrance-exam cultures of China and South Korea shown as the extreme case of education deciding a life.

beats.title: State standards and one federal exception
beats.summary: One participant pointed to Virginia's Standards of Learning and the Texas STAAR tests as proof that standards are set state by state, and described the cost of moving between them: children arriving from a high-performing state ahead of the local curriculum, then playing catch-up after the next move, with one child in that family losing a year of math placement in the process. That participant would prefer a national curriculum, or at least a federal standard, because states are being treated almost as separate countries. Another answered that the federal government has kept out of education standards exactly once: after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, a STEM priority program eventually housed in the Education Department fostered state standards at primary, secondary and post-secondary level. Beyond that, the federal role has been to insist that whatever standard a state sets is equally accessible across its population, and to fund underserved communities where property-tax-based school finance falls short. The facilitator tied this back to the earlier chat line about separate but equal, and warned that inequality, once formed, takes two or three generations to unwind.
beats.pullQuote: We're almost treating each State as a different country based on, you know, their own curriculum
beats.slideHint: Policies slide: a strip contrasting state testing regimes (Standards of Learning in Virginia, STAAR in Texas, Department of Defense schools in the middle) with a timeline callout for the post-Sputnik STEM program as the single federal intervention in standards, and a footnote on property-tax-based school funding.

beats.title: Pittsburgh, and what a government values
beats.summary: One participant described Pittsburgh's particular case: legally desegregated in 1981, but the shape of the city and its suburbs left segregation standing, and a high school was placed between two suburbs to force new district lines, which people resented at the time and, that participant believes, resent still. Homeschooling their own children, the same participant hears from church and community families about strong programs and troubled kids inside the same buildings, and warned that anything adopted now is a pebble dropped in water whose ripples take time to return. Another participant picked up the desegregation thread from a recent Malcolm Gladwell book on the Ivy League and what the culture says about education, its title garbled in the recording: schools were desegregated for students but not for teachers, African American teachers were largely dismissed, and minority students were left without a teacher who looked like them or saw things differently, an effect that participant said is still felt. That led on to what a government's national programs reveal about what it values, and to the worry that dissolving the department shows education is valued less than assumed, closing with the note that Canada has no federal oversight of education at all; everything sits with the provinces.
beats.pullQuote: What? What does the Us. Government value? And it I feel like things that have a national program are kind of like showing what our country places most value on.
beats.slideHint: Root Causes slide: a Pittsburgh timeline (legal desegregation in 1981, a high school sited between two suburbs, tension that outlasted the order) beside a 'desegregated for students, not for teachers' panel, with the pebble-in-the-water image for lag time and a one-line comparison of where oversight sits in Canada and the United States.

beats.title: School districts, stipends, and homeschooling
beats.summary: One participant relayed a teacher's account from a school on a base: staff could tell, without testing, whether a student arriving from a given state would be ahead or behind. Another said their family chose their rented house for its school district, knowing which schools it fed before the move, and named a growing turn to homeschooling among families dissatisfied with what their children were getting, with quality varying sharply from one household to the next. The same participant then described an engineered kind of sorting: International Baccalaureate programs placed in the lowest-ranked high school in each of three Virginia cities, which lifts that school's reported scores, and stipends that draw teachers to the most challenged schools, so that where a teacher works carries its own stigma or status. The first participant set out why their family homeschools: safety, rumors about the next school, bad influences and peer groups, and a felt absence of structure in morals and ethics, alongside the freedom to travel and to substitute practical life learning, cooking, shopping, applying math in the shop, for book knowledge alone.
beats.pullQuote: So teachers, if they need money or they need to be paid more, are going to work at some of the the more challenged schools.
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide split three ways - choosing a home by school district, International Baccalaureate placement lifting a weak school's numbers, stipends and stigma following teachers - with a fourth column on homeschooling motives: safety, morals and ethics, flexibility, practical learning.

beats.title: Communities as curriculum
beats.summary: The facilitator turned to opportunities. If education falls to states and communities, then morals and ethics need not be left to an institution to define, and the diversity of the United States means communities could shape cultural identity themselves, with Hispanic, Black, Asian, Jewish and other voices saying what their own heritage means. One participant argued that the pot has been stirred: immigration went almost unspoken until it was raised, education may be the same, and polarized argument beats stagnation if it reinvigorates the question of how to invest in children and at what level. The facilitator replied that the Lyceum holds difficult conversations by leaning into the problem rather than into political identity or ideology, and offered Canada as a worked example, the land acknowledgement and a Truth and Reconciliation Commission dated in the session to 2016 making First Nations, Metis and Inuit history a taught mandate, filling a gap in the national story. Another participant posted gratitude in the chat for living and learning on the stolen lands of the Squamish, Tsleil-Waututh and Musqueam Nations. The participant who had spoken of the stirred pot then opened the language question: states with heavy immigration, a curriculum delivered in English, English as a second language, refugees arriving already at school age.
beats.pullQuote: We don't lean into ideology, we lean into the problem that exists.
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide 'communities as curriculum': three bullets (morals and ethics decided locally, cultural voices naming their own heritage, difficult conversation better than stagnation) beside a Canada panel on land acknowledgement and the Truth and Reconciliation teaching mandate as a model for filling a gap in national history.

beats.title: What a border does to a qualification
beats.summary: A participant working on a project with migrant women named the challenge the group had not touched: a lawyer in their own country, cleaning houses here. Speaking the local language is a matter of respect and the gate to everything else, they said, since a person cannot live twenty years in a country without it and, without it, college and university stay closed, though keeping one's own culture was never in question. They also named the harder disappointment, arriving in a country that says it is not racist and finding racism anyway, with going back not an option. The facilitator summarized the gap: a professional license or degree stops counting on arrival, a successful life restarts from the bottom, and language itself blocks both the new culture and the next job, so education is needed to close it. Another participant added the soldiers they had met who hold the equivalent of a master's degree and enlisted because nobody would recognize their qualifications, and noted that international agencies exist to credit prior study. A further voice posted in the chat about growing up in New Jersey learning everything there is to know about the Lenape.
beats.pullQuote: It's almost like they're starting their life all over again, and they're trying to build back up and the language barrier itself could be a huge obstacle
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide 'what a border does to a qualification': a three-step drop (qualified professional, unrecognized credential, entry-level work) with language shown as the gate across all three, and a side panel naming credential-evaluation agencies and language leveling as existing remedies.

beats.title: Assimilation, welcome, and a steward for the inquiry
beats.summary: One participant told of a well-educated colleague in the Navy, already speaking three languages while becoming an American citizen, and of shutting down shipmates who said that colleague did not even speak English. The welcoming instinct of some people in a great land, that participant said, often makes the immigration experience less than desirable, with each group assuming its rights supersede the next arrivals'. From the same family history came the cost of speed: German-speaking parents who forbade German in the house so that a grandparent would assimilate quickly, and two generations on, a descendant in the circle who cannot speak it and has lost the commonality with people of another country or religion. Another participant stepped away in the chat. The facilitator then put the call to action, so that the evening's collective knowledge would not simply disperse. One participant volunteered to look into how curriculum is developed and whether citizens and parents can be given a voice in what their children are taught. The facilitator joined that inquiry, saying that a thesis in human development sits in exactly that space and was part of the impetus for the group, and kept the team open to others. A third volunteered as well and offered to pass the inquiry on. A fourth, declining to speak, wrote instead that part of their own education came from adults who were not technically educators, which the facilitator read out and extended to elders and technical experts whose skill should not be dismissed for want of letters after a name.
beats.pullQuote: He speaks 3 languages. You barely speak one.
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead slide: the call to action stated as a continuing inquiry with a shared product that others can add to, the volunteers listed unnamed with one line each and the fourth place marked withheld, and a side panel headed 'educators without the title' drawn from the chat.

beats.title: Learning reflection and the fellowship circle
beats.summary: One of the hosts posted the closing survey, the learning reflection, into the chat with thanks for the group's participation, and the facilitator put the QR code on screen and left it up rather than rushing anyone, then opened the fellowship circle, where the floor goes round one last time and silence counts as an offering. One participant, borrowing another member's habit of writing notes first, thanked everyone and pressed the point home: as much was learned from four colleagues from those service years, whose names are withheld here, as from any year in any classroom. Another said the classroom format holds their attention but doubted it has a future, since stories are how an adult learns best, and wondered aloud what that means for children. A third thanked the circle for the range of perspectives in a respectful environment. The facilitator called the evening an example of what such conversations could look like in communities anywhere without descending into conflict, promised products from it, and named the next Lyceum for the following month. Answering the earlier chat proposal for further discussion, the facilitator explained the six-month reflection, when stewards report back on their inquiries and the group weighs in, and listed those carrying this one forward: three from the room, and a fourth, a family member who was not present, withheld here.
beats.pullQuote: I learn here a lot from stories, and I think, as an adult, that is the best way to learn.
beats.slideHint: Post-Survey slide with the Learning Reflection QR code and a chat-link fallback, then a Fellowship Circle slide naming silence as an offering, then a closing slide with the six-month reflection cycle, who is carrying this inquiry forward, and a placeholder for next month's Lyceum.

inquiries.callToAction: The call to action stayed with the whole circle rather than one champion: each participant is asked to find a way to build the community in their own sphere of influence, from inviting someone to a Lyceum to watching for local events where the work can be introduced, and the facilitator will follow up by email. One participant volunteered to forward the recorded conference presentation to a rabbi, a conduit to counterparts in other religious organizations. Another offered to share that same conference video with a university professor and with further contacts as ideas surface. A third plans to approach the Common Ground Scholar network of clergy to see who is willing to amplify the message in their own communities, will create social media content from this and earlier Lyceums through the summer, and will add and visualize connections to partner organizations on the website. A fourth will list past Lyceums there in digestible, searchable form with ways to volunteer. Shinrin-yoku flyers will be redrawn in bright hand-drawn nature art with the nature games named on them. A young participant suggested seeking permission to post nonprofit flyers at a school, and the circle put forward a Praxium podcast and short Lyceum clips as content to make next.

storyboard.logline: After an eight-month pause, a Praxium circle spread from Lima to Los Angeles gave an evening, and then some, to one question: how to grow the learning community.
storyboard.arcNotes: The session opened tightly scripted - norms, pre-survey, land gratitude, introductions - and stayed personal longer than usual because eight months of life had piled up: a retirement, an 80-hour coaching certification, a thesis nearing its end, a family living abroad in Lima. The discussion opened up twice. First when the questions were handed to the young participants at the table, whose answers - a school fundraiser run drawing two hundred people, posters cleared with the school, bright hand-drawn nature pictures, games named on the flyer - reframed outreach from adult marketing into something a child would pick up. Second when a participant asked why anyone should have to leave the country for cultural experience, which turned the room inward: Habitat for Humanity in Los Angeles, immigrants already arriving in America, one subway stop between worlds in the Bronx, an older neighbor's steps shoveled in Pittsburgh. Convergence came from a communications-theory frame offered late in the evening - person to person, then groups, then broad social media, run simultaneously with tailored messaging - which the participant who had opened the inward turn adopted explicitly at the close. The last third narrowed to obstacles that are practical rather than ideological: crowded inboxes, complaint without solutions, scarce attention. The call to action was left deliberately undelegated, owned by everyone in their own sphere of influence with follow-up by email, and the closing circle ran past time through vulnerability, similarities over wedges, heart rather than regulation, and the website roadmap. Reviewer notes: speaker labels are unreliable from about @1:45:51 to the end, including the block at @1:50:25, so who said what in that stretch was read from context rather than from the label; contributions by the two minors are recorded only as coming from a young participant, and one attendee's health remark and a visiting veteran's identifying details were left out.

beats.title: Reopening after eight months
beats.summary: The facilitator opened by welcoming the circle to the first Lyceum in about eight months, the last having been in November 2025, and read the structural norms for a shared purpose meeting - every person a peer, every voice welcome, safe and respectful comment, seek commonality while respecting difference - asking that the young guests present be encouraged to speak. The ninety-minute agenda was walked through, with the note that the question was pre-determined, so no time would go to deliberating what to discuss. A two-question pre-survey went up by QR code asking whether each person needed to be helped, hugged or heard and how the circle could help; answers were read aloud at one table, one participant observed that their own responses were no longer anonymous, and another offered a hug across the call.

beats.title: Present circle and land gratitude
beats.summary: The facilitator led the opening presence as a deliberate stop to the day's hustle, Monday's meetings and tomorrow's problems, orienting the circle toward place, family, self and children. Standing in for the usual Canadian land acknowledgement, the gratitude went to the Allegheny, Ohio and Monongahela rivers in Pennsylvania, with Monongahela translated as 'fallen banks' and each person invited to consider the heritage of their own ground. The facilitator then modeled the shared understanding round first: Army service, and three months in Europe in support of Ukraine since the last gathering, with home defined as the people one feels connected to rather than a fixed address.
beats.pullQuote: home is just people that I feel connected to
beats.slideHint: Opening / Present Circle slide: land acknowledgement text naming the Allegheny, Ohio and Monongahela watershed with the 'fallen banks' translation, and the three shared-understanding prompts (cultural background, where you call home, what has happened since the last Lyceum).

beats.title: Lima, young voices, and coaching
beats.summary: A participant joining from Lima, Peru introduced the group gathered there, where a two-day conference on spirituality and religion in society had just finished, and framed the stay as a chance to build community in Latin America. The young participants were then given space to introduce themselves in their own words, and one answered the cultural identity prompt by claiming many cultures and putting home wherever the family is. Another participant reported from Texas on completing an 80-hour executive, life and goal-setting coaching course they had first been skeptical of, valuing it for drawing out people's own realizations. The same voice named Parents in Action as the newest channel, focused on developing children for what is coming, and reported more allies and network than at the last Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: thank you ... for putting this on and creating the space for us to practice the Lyceum as this endeavor for shared purpose
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding slide: the three prompts small in the corner, a Lima photo strip for the conference on spirituality and religion in society, and a callout box for the two newer channels - coaching (80-hour certification) and Parents in Action.

beats.title: Retirement, service, and a thesis
beats.summary: One participant announced a retirement, recommended it to anyone working toward it, and described taking over maintenance at their synagogue on the grounds that the congregation has plenty of lawyers, doctors and judges but few people who can drive a nail straight. Another named retired Army life as the strongest thread in a mixed cultural background and said they are still trying to make sense of a lot of uncertainty. A third attendee, showing only as an unrecognized string of letters, was invited to come off mic: born in Belize and long settled in Los Angeles, entering the tail end of a thesis on Belizean women and mother-daughter bonding. Every introduction converged on the same answer to where home is.
beats.pullQuote: No matter where I am, my family is where home is.
beats.slideHint: Shared Understanding continued: round-robin list with one line for each person, the repeated answer 'home is where the family is' pulled out as a large callout, and a small footnote that a device name hid an attendee until they introduced themselves on mic.

beats.title: The map and the question
beats.summary: A colored world map placed the circle across the United States, Europe, the Caribbean and South America, used to make the point that what is a problem for one person may not be a problem for another. The facilitator walked the sequence of inquiry the evening would follow: theories and concepts, application, sources and inputs, opportunities and challenges, then a call to action. The topic was tied to the Praxium's first annual meeting at the beginning of June, called a milestone, and the single question for the night was set. The facilitator also noted a personal arc, from wondering two years ago what there was to add to now guiding this Lyceum.
beats.pullQuote: how do we grow the Praxium learning community? How do we get more people involved?
beats.slideHint: Two slides: colored world map with attendee locations pinned and the Caribbean inset called out, then Today's Inquiry - 'How do we grow the Praxium learning community?' - with the sequence of inquiry listed down the side as the evening's roadmap.

beats.title: Lived experience and trusted conduits
beats.summary: One participant argued the message can grow because it is fundamentally about humanity, and that the group's lived experience carries further than theory does, reporting consistently warm reception with no substantive pushback, especially for coaching aimed at veterans moving into civilian communities. Another put the same question to the young participants at the table, asking where they had seen families and community members show up at school rather than only students. One of them named the Terry Fox run, a lap-based school fundraiser for cancer research drawing roughly two hundred people, which produced the night's first concrete channel: local events and schools. A further participant then described discussing the video of the Lima conference presentation with a rabbi that day and forwarding it that evening, treating the rabbi as a conduit to counterparts in other religious organizations, while the facilitator pointed to the existing Facebook and LinkedIn work and short clips cut from Lyceums.
beats.pullQuote: We're tired of sitting in the passenger seat getting told, hey, this is where we're going. No, we want to get in the driver's seat and we want to lead.
beats.slideHint: Theories and Concepts slide: bullets for message rooted in humanity, lived experience over theory, reception to date, veteran transition coaching, and local events and schools as an untapped audience (Terry Fox run, about 200 attendees), with 'driver's seat, not passenger seat' as the banner line.

beats.title: Flyers a kid would read
beats.summary: A participant asked the young participants how to reach children about the Shinrin Yoku forest bathing offering, a six-month project whose flyers and email lists only reach adults. Their answers were specific: posters put up at school with permission, bright hand-drawn nature pictures instead of adult-oriented documents, and naming the nature games on the flyer so children know games are part of the immersion. The same participant noted that learners in their sixties and seventies already run alongside children at these events, and a further suggestion that the material include everyone led back to the mission language of fellowship through diversity. The facilitator added mediums beyond social media - a scoreboard advertisement at a Pirates game, radio, a Praxium podcast running interviews - and another participant asked permission to share the conference video with a university professor, which was granted without restriction.
beats.pullQuote: if you're talking about making hand-drawn images of things that kids would naturally want to see, you're right
beats.slideHint: Channels and Amplifiers slide: two columns, trusted conduits (clergy, professors, veteran networks, shared video) and mediums (Facebook, LinkedIn, shorts, podcast, radio, event advertising), plus a mock kid-facing Shinrin Yoku flyer - bright colors, hand-drawn nature, games named, multiple generations shown.

beats.title: Framing outward, building in Lima
beats.summary: The facilitator opened the application section on making a message land outside America, using Pittsburgh dialect ('yinz' where others say 'y'all') and World Cup visitors discovering ranch dressing as examples of how accidentally local a message can be. A participant described Alternative Peru, the nonprofit another member of the circle found, whose guided excursions deliberately skip the standard Cusco and Machu Picchu itinerary. Young participants recounted a week of community building in Lima: homework help and play at a children's library, a dance hall mixing indigenous and Latin music, a meal in a local family's home where the hosts asked what the visitors made of Peru, and a boatyard where they met the local craftsman who builds most of the boats. The participant who had introduced Alternative Peru drew the summarizing point that these are the things residents actually do, and that curiosity and broken Spanish were enough to start the conversations.
beats.pullQuote: we've gone to a children's library to help out with, like, their homework, and we've been playing with them
beats.slideHint: Application slide: 'how is this handled around the world' with the Alternative Peru non-tourist model listed against the standard tourist itinerary, four Lima examples as icons (library, dance hall, shared meal, boatyard), and a caption on messaging that travels past its own dialect.

beats.title: Citizens of the world
beats.summary: The facilitator described meeting nonprofit organizations while in Europe that act as a central hub between donors and people in need, and using those conversations to introduce the Praxium's work with veterans and across generations. Asked how the family living abroad explains ending up in Peru, the participant joining from there said the answer given is that they are citizens of the world, learning and loving together by doing it physically rather than talking about it. That participant framed travel as resilience practice and suggested that a family who travels can role model the practice for families who have not considered it. Another participant and the facilitator both affirmed the shaping effect of such experience, the facilitator recalling helping build houses in Mexico and needing a translator to connect.
beats.pullQuote: I've been really telling people that we're citizens of the world, and that we're trying to learn and love together
beats.slideHint: Application continued: 'citizens of the world' as the header, with a three-step ladder (exposure, experience, resilience) and a side panel on nonprofits as donor-to-resource hubs and interconnecting older and younger generations.

beats.title: The next neighborhood over
beats.summary: Prompted by the land acknowledgement being brought home to Pennsylvania, one participant turned the inquiry inward and asked how to encourage people into a different neighborhood in their own city instead of a foreign country. The facilitator framed members as ambassadors for a better community and proposed using social media to show where each person is and how they are connected to the land they live on. Another participant described volunteering with Habitat for Humanity on the west side of Los Angeles and argued that immigrants already arriving in America should be made to feel welcome, because the communities needing help are right here. The facilitator matched that with shoveling snow and helping older neighbors without vehicles reach appointments through a hard Pittsburgh winter, and a third participant with Pelham Parkway in the Bronx, where one subway stop moved you between Jewish, Italian and Chinese neighborhoods.
beats.pullQuote: you really only had to go a subway stop down the way and you were in a different world
beats.slideHint: Application - Cultural exchange at home: reframe banner 'you do not have to leave the country to cross a culture', with three worked examples (Habitat for Humanity in Los Angeles, welcoming immigrants already here, a Bronx subway stop between neighborhoods) and a small prompt asking each attendee to name one neighborhood they have never visited.

beats.title: Three fronts at once
beats.summary: One participant supplied the evening's organizing frame from communications theory: person-to-person engagement as the building block, then groups and affinity groups, then the much broader community reachable through social media. Assessing the Praxium as working mostly person-to-person with some group and social media effect, the same voice argued the three have to run simultaneously, with messaging tailored to each audience while the core message holds. The facilitator connected that to holding public Lyceums in a commonplace room that needs no Teams link, computer, tablet or internet, where a person can walk in and be helped, heard or hugged. That closed the loop back to the pre-survey question of how each person arrives.
beats.pullQuote: But doing all three simultaneously is probably the most effective way to grow the effort overall.
beats.slideHint: Scaling model slide: three-tier diagram (individual, group and affinity, broad social media) with 'run all three at once, tailor the messaging, hold the core message' beneath, and a side note on in-person public Lyceums with no technology barrier tied back to helped / heard / hugged.

beats.title: Common ground and veterans
beats.summary: One participant recast the sources question as building the network and the team on top of several years of groundwork, and marketing the group's relevance and impact on communities. Another named the Common Ground Scholar collaborative, whose two-day conference drew over two hundred participants including Buddhist, Orthodox Christian, Muslim and Jewish clergy, as a network worth asking to amplify the message in their own communities. That same participant recounted a dinner conversation with a veteran who keeps military service off a professional profile but volunteered it once the Praxium's message came up, and the W. E. B. Du Bois challenge, written from Ghana, to veterans who fought for democracy abroad; the takeaway offered was the common ground network plus veterans groups, with service out of uniform as the framing. A third participant said the conversation kept generating more places to share the video, the facilitator pointed to existing small groups such as a Saturday running group as ready-made openings, and a fourth called a group run forest bathing on the road.
beats.pullQuote: you fought for liberty abroad, but why can't you do it at home?
beats.slideHint: Sources and Inputs slide: who and what is needed - Common Ground Scholar and interfaith clergy, veteran service organizations, the Kintsugi campaign, existing affinity groups such as running and fellowship groups - with the Du Bois challenge as the pull quote and 'service, just not in uniform' as the framing line.

beats.title: Complaint, universality, and saying hello
beats.summary: The facilitator described the military family skill of getting a household linked into a community, a religious group or some fellowship on arrival so nobody sits staring at four walls, and noted how much the younger generation struggles to build that kind of connection, then named a habit seen in military culture and beyond - complaining without solutions - and proposed answering it by asking people how they would actually fix the problem if handed authority for a day, with community as the honest answer. One participant held that the human experience is universal wherever you go, the same fear, joy, need for belonging and wanting the best for your family, and only the difficulty varies; that participant described greeting strangers in the street in a country of birth, missing that for years, and now saying hello first even when nobody answers, because their own part has been done. Another added that a first hello can open an entire dialogue, and that whatever problem someone is stuck on, somebody out there has already lived it and holds wisdom worth asking for.
beats.pullQuote: most of the time it's more of just complaining without solutions
beats.slideHint: Opportunities slide split in two: on the left the pattern to break (complaint without solutions, four walls on arrival, younger generation out of practice), on the right the low-cost moves (say hello first, ask how they would fix it, assume someone has already solved it), under the header 'the human experience is universal'.

beats.title: Inbox noise and priorities
beats.summary: The facilitator turned to opportunities and challenges and named communicating meaningfully with people who are all in a hurry as the hardest of them. One participant sharpened it to inboxes full of people demanding attention and competing for time and resources, and asked how anything rises above that noise. In reply, the facilitator said no magical filter exists, and that three months away from a phone had shown how few things actually matter, retelling a lecture demonstration in which golf balls stand for the few big priorities, gravel and sand for everything that fills the gaps, and a poured beer for the room left to have fun. The practice described was writing down a top three and slowing down deliberately - forest bathing, a walk with a podcast, a quiet cup of coffee - and another participant said writing things down and forest bathing both work for them.
beats.pullQuote: how do you separate the wheat from the chaff
beats.slideHint: Challenges slide: bullets for attention scarcity, inbox noise, busy schedules and the difficulty of being heard, paired with a jar graphic (golf balls, gravel, sand, beer) and the practices column - top three written down, mindfulness, time in nature.

beats.title: A collective call to action
beats.summary: Rather than naming one champion for the topic, the facilitator made the call to action collective and said it would come as a follow-up email: each person decides how they will contribute to building the community in their own sphere of influence. The offers already on the table were named - sharing the conference video, inviting people to a Lyceum, reaching out locally, posting to social media - with a challenge to everyone to make the difference where they are. One participant answered simply that they would do it. Another adopted the three fronts named earlier in the evening explicitly for the summer, noted that families off school spend more time on social media, and committed to creating Lyceum content for the Facebook and LinkedIn presence heading into fall.
beats.pullQuote: it almost seems like it's a collective responsibility and a collective call to action
beats.slideHint: Way Ahead / Call to Action slide: 'In what way can you contribute to building this community?' with the four offers already on the table listed beneath, the follow-up email named as the mechanism, and a summer-into-fall timeline strip for the social media content.

beats.title: Reflection survey and gratitude
beats.summary: The learning reflection questionnaire went out as the last slide, answered anonymously and explicitly not used to track anyone down, with the link dropped into chat for whoever could not scan it. Opening the final round, the facilitator thanked the circle for the chance to guide the evening after eight months apart, and noted who was joining from where, including a family in Peru and a colleague coming off a field rotation. Recalling work with international communities that had drifted from what they could build together toward what they could get out of it, the facilitator described telling them to imagine instead what they could all do together, credited the Lyceum's mix of places and experiences for both its camaraderie and its reach, then joked about sour Pittsburgh first impressions and the steel companies that left.
beats.pullQuote: if you could do this by yourself, like, imagine what we could all do together
beats.slideHint: Post-Survey slide: learning reflection QR code with the chat-link fallback, the two prompts (what spoke to you today, what should the next Lyceum take up), a note that answers are anonymous, and a closing-round marker underneath.

beats.title: Vulnerability and shared similarities
beats.summary: One participant named pride and the human wish to be seen as good enough as the material the circle is working with, and said the hard part is holding love and vulnerability alongside the work of meeting people where they are; asked to repeat it, that participant said it again. Still working through the questionnaire on a shifted screen, the same voice asked forgiveness for being a little technically challenged, then, invited to give closing remarks, picked up the Bronx story told earlier by another participant: two blocks over in New York City is another world, so you do not have to travel around the world to see the world, and much of the change the group wants can happen inside America. A further participant agreed and argued that focusing on similarities and mutual help, rather than driving wedges, is what keeps a collective from breaking into smaller groups that argue and bicker.
beats.pullQuote: you don't have to travel around the world to actually see the world
beats.slideHint: Closing Circle slide one: two facing panels - 'be vulnerable, meet people where they are' and 'similarities over wedges' - with the restated reframe across the bottom, that seeing the world can start two blocks away.

beats.title: Heart, and the website roadmap
beats.summary: The facilitator observed that when the person in charge is the one handing out division cards, looking past the divisions gets harder, and one participant answered that a community should not need laws and regulations to behave decently; the facilitator named heart for service as the thing underneath. That same participant also said they had been reserved but feel more and more comfortable in their share each time they come back, and the circle said it was glad to have that experience and those studies on the calls. Another participant called the group's real contribution the creation of space for dialogue, where people who sit at different points on the political spectrum can air differences without cutting each other's throats, and the facilitator added that technology has cost some of the younger generation the mannerisms for starting such a conversation. The closing remarks came back to the Praxium's calls to action through the Kintsugi campaign, the Lyceum and social media; one participant added the website work on visualizing connections to partner organizations and another the plan to list previous Lyceums in a digestible, searchable form with ways for people to volunteer, before thanks and goodnights slightly over time.
beats.pullQuote: We shouldn't need laws and regulations.
beats.slideHint: Final slide pair: the Praxium offerings as calls to action (Lyceum, Kintsugi, Shinrin Yoku, social media), then the website roadmap - partner organization map, searchable archive of previous Lyceums, volunteer sign-up - with a goodnight line and the next Lyceum placeholder.
